observations.title: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys
observations.text:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi. Improper Certificate Validation

observations.title: Wasmtime: Bit-packing in Cranelift compiler causes silent overflow and miscompilation
observations.text:
## Summary

In Wasmtime prior to v43, the Cranelift compiler backend bit-packs its SSA value indices in a way that can result in silent overflow in release builds, and result in incorrect value references in the IR resulting in arbitrary miscompilation. A very large Wasm function body, or one that is specially crafted to use many SSA values, can use this to force type-confusion or other arbitrary side-effects and escape the sandbox.

Cranelift was changed in Wasmtime v43 to use a full `u32` index, with checks if that limit is exceeded, and so is no longer susceptible to this bug.

## Impact

A Wasmtime engine with default settings (using the Cranelift backend) on any architecture/platform could experience a sandbox escape from a specially-crafted Wasm module.

## Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19
observations.fix: upgrade wasmtime to 36.0.19; upgrade wasmtime to 43.0.0

observations.title: Laravel TokenGuard authentication bypass through non-string API credentials
observations.text:
Laravel's built-in TokenGuard, **when configured with a standard token-based API guard**, may be bypassed to authenticate as an arbitrary existing user without knowledge of their valid API token. 

**Under certain database configurations (MySQL/MariaDB)** an attacker can submit a specially crafted, non-string credential value that is mishandled during the authentication lookup, causing the underlying query to match an unintended user record rather than failing authentication as expected.

### Impact
An unauthenticated attacker may authenticate as another user without possessing that user's API token, leading to authentication bypass and account takeover on any route protected by the affected guard. Improper Authentication Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input

observations.title: Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
observations.text:
### Summary

The main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented [design](https://electrum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html#does-electrum-trust-servers). [0]

However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:
- when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,

- Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).
- The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.
- If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.

## Summary

When running with the Cranelift compiler backend on an aarch64 target, Wasmtime can compile a Wasm module with more than ~256k targets on one `br_table` instruction in a way that results in an incorrect conditional branch target. observations.text:
## Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.
